title: Critical Thinking Academy
description: Develop the skills to reason clearly, evaluate evidence, spot fallacies, and make well-reasoned decisions.

lessons.title: What Is an Argument?
lessons.explanation: In critical thinking, an 'argument' is not a fight — it is a set of reasons (called premises) offered in support of a conclusion. A good argument has true premises and the conclusion follows logically from them.
lessons.example:
Premise 1: All humans are mortal.
Premise 2: Socrates is a human.
Conclusion: Therefore, Socrates is mortal.

This is a VALID argument — if both premises are true, the conclusion must be true.
lessons.exercise: Identify the premises and conclusion: 'Dogs are loyal animals. My pet Max is a dog. Therefore, Max is loyal.'
lessons.exercise_answer: Premise 1: Dogs are loyal animals. Premise 2: Max is a dog. Conclusion: Max is loyal.

quiz.q: In an argument, what are the reasons given to support the conclusion called?
A valid argument means:
options: If the premises are true, the conclusion must follow

lessons.title: Deductive vs Inductive Reasoning
lessons.explanation:
DEDUCTIVE reasoning: if the premises are true, the conclusion is GUARANTEED to be true. It moves from general to specific.

INDUCTIVE reasoning: the premises make the conclusion PROBABLE but not guaranteed. It moves from specific observations to general conclusions.

ABDUCTIVE reasoning: inferring the most likely explanation for an observation. Used by doctors, detectives, and scientists. 'The best explanation for these symptoms is…'
lessons.example:
Deductive: All birds have wings. A robin is a bird. → A robin has wings. (Certain)

Inductive: I've seen 100 swans. All 100 were white. → All swans are probably white. (Probable — but black swans do exist!)

Abductive: The patient has a fever and sore throat. The best explanation is a bacterial infection.
lessons.exercise: Is this deductive or inductive? 'Every time I eat spicy food, I get a stomach ache. So spicy food probably causes stomach aches for me.'
lessons.exercise_answer: Inductive — it moves from specific observations to a general conclusion about probability.

logical_fallacies.label: Logical Fallacies
logical_fallacies.description: Recognise flawed arguments and errors in reasoning.

lessons.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
lessons.explanation: Ad hominem (Latin: 'to the person') is attacking the person making the argument instead of the argument itself. Even if someone has bad qualities, their argument could still be correct.
lessons.example: 'You shouldn't listen to her climate change advice — she drives a car!' This attacks the person, not the evidence for climate change.
lessons.exercise: Is this an ad hominem? 'Your argument for eating vegetables is wrong because you're overweight.' Explain.
lessons.exercise_answer: Yes — this attacks the person's weight rather than addressing whether vegetables are healthy.

quiz.q: Ad hominem means attacking:
Which is an ad hominem fallacy?
options: 'You can't trust her opinion on healthy eating — she's unhealthy herself'

lessons.title: Straw Man Fallacy
lessons.explanation: A straw man argument misrepresents or exaggerates someone's position to make it easier to attack. The 'straw man' is a fake, weaker version of the original argument.
lessons.example:
Person A: 'We should have some regulations on fast food advertising to children.'
Person B: 'So you want to ban all unhealthy food and control what people eat?'

Person B has distorted Person A's position into something extreme.
lessons.exercise: Identify the straw man: 'She said we should recycle more. But of course she wants to BAN all plastic forever and make everyone live without modern convenience!'
lessons.exercise_answer: The straw man is the claim that she wants to 'ban all plastic forever' — she only suggested recycling more.

quiz.q: A straw man fallacy involves:
options: Misrepresenting someone's argument to attack it more easily

lessons.title: False Dichotomy (Either/Or Fallacy)
lessons.explanation: A false dichotomy presents only two options when more options exist. 'You're either with us or against us' ignores the middle ground and other possibilities.
lessons.example: 'You either love eating meat or you hate the environment.' This ignores the many people who eat meat but still care about the environment, or vegetarians who harm the environment in other ways.
lessons.exercise: Identify the false dichotomy: 'Either you study 8 hours a day or you'll fail your exams.'
lessons.exercise_answer: This is a false dichotomy — there are many study strategies between 0 and 8 hours that lead to exam success.

evidence_evaluation.label: Evaluating Evidence
evidence_evaluation.description: Learn to assess the quality and reliability of information.

lessons.title: Primary vs Secondary Sources
lessons.explanation:
A PRIMARY source is original, first-hand material — a diary, a scientific study, a photograph, an interview. A SECONDARY source interprets or analyses primary sources — a textbook, a news article, a documentary.

PEER REVIEW: The process by which scientific studies are evaluated by other experts before publication. Peer-reviewed research is considered more reliable than non-peer-reviewed sources.
lessons.example:
Primary: Einstein's original 1905 paper on special relativity.
Secondary: A textbook chapter explaining Einstein's theory of relativity.
lessons.exercise: Is this primary or secondary? 'A newspaper article reporting on a new study about sleep and memory.'
lessons.exercise_answer: Secondary — it reports on another source (the study). The actual study is the primary source.

quiz.q: Which is a primary source?
options: A textbook chapter about World War II
A documentary about World War II

quiz.q: Peer review means:
options: Evaluation by other experts before publication

lessons.title: Recognising Bias
lessons.explanation:
Bias is a tendency to favour one perspective unfairly. Sources can have bias due to: financial interests (funded by a company), political views, cultural background, or selection bias (only showing evidence that supports one conclusion).

CONFIRMATION BIAS: The tendency to search for and accept information that confirms what we already believe, while ignoring contradictory evidence.
lessons.example: A study on the health effects of sugar, funded by a sugar company, might be biased toward downplaying negative effects. Confirmation bias leads us to share news articles that match our existing views without checking if they are accurate.
lessons.exercise: Identify the potential bias: 'A report by an oil company concludes that fossil fuels are not the main cause of climate change.'
lessons.exercise_answer: The oil company has a financial interest in the conclusion — this is a clear potential bias. Independent scientific consensus should be sought.

quiz.q: Confirmation bias means:
options: Seeking information that confirms your existing beliefs

quiz.q: Which factor is LEAST likely to introduce bias into a study?
options: Funded by a company that benefits from the result
Reports only results supporting one view
Researcher has a strong personal opinion

scientific_method.label: Scientific Method
scientific_method.description: How science works: hypothesis, experiment, evidence, and revision.

lessons.title: Hypothesis, Experiment, and Evidence
lessons.explanation:
The scientific method is a systematic approach to knowledge:

1. OBSERVATION: Notice a phenomenon or question.
2. HYPOTHESIS: Form a testable, falsifiable prediction. A good hypothesis can be proven wrong.
3. EXPERIMENT: Test the hypothesis by controlling variables. Change one variable at a time (independent variable) and measure the effect (dependent variable). Control variables remain constant.
4. DATA COLLECTION: Record results objectively.
5. ANALYSIS: Look for patterns. Does the evidence support or contradict the hypothesis?
6. CONCLUSION: Was the hypothesis supported? What does this tell us? Can results be replicated?

FALSIFIABILITY (Karl Popper): A statement is scientific only if there is a possible observation that could prove it wrong. 'All swans are white' is falsifiable — finding one black swan disproves it.
lessons.example:
Hypothesis: Plants grow faster with music.
Experiment: Grow 20 identical plants — 10 with music, 10 in silence, all other conditions identical.
Result: No significant difference in growth rates.
Conclusion: No evidence that music affects growth rate under these conditions. The hypothesis is not supported.
lessons.exercise: Is this a good scientific hypothesis? 'Some plants grow faster when they feel happy.' Explain.
lessons.exercise_answer: No — 'feel happy' is not measurable or falsifiable. A good hypothesis would be: 'Plants exposed to music grow taller in 4 weeks than plants in silence' — this is specific and testable.

quiz.q: The independent variable in an experiment is:
options: The variable that is deliberately changed

quiz.q: Falsifiability means:
options: A statement that is always false
A statement that could be proven wrong by observation
A result that cannot be replicated
A hypothesis that has been disproven

fact_checking.label: Fact Checking
fact_checking.description: Techniques for verifying claims, detecting misinformation, and cross-referencing sources.

lessons.title: How to Fact-Check: SIFT Method
lessons.explanation:
Fake news is false or misleading information spread as news. Use the SIFT method:

• STOP — Don't react immediately or share without thinking.
• INVESTIGATE the source — Who made this claim? What is their track record, bias, and motivation?
• FIND better coverage — Do reliable, independent sources confirm the claim?
• TRACE claims, quotes, and media to their original context.

Other tools:
• LATERAL READING: Open new browser tabs to check the source from the outside rather than reading the source itself.
• REVERSE IMAGE SEARCH: Check if an image was taken in a different time/place than claimed.
• Check established fact-checking organisations.

Red flags: Anonymous sources, extreme emotional headlines, no date, no author, urging you to share urgently.
lessons.example: A viral post claims: 'Scientists prove eating chocolate every day cures cancer!' Red flags: no named scientists, no link to a study, extreme claim, emotional headline. Lateral reading: no established news organisation has reported this claim.
lessons.exercise: Apply SIFT to: 'Government secretly adds chemicals to drinking water to control minds, leaked document reveals!'
lessons.exercise_answer: STOP — the headline is designed to provoke. INVESTIGATE: Is this a known, credible source? FIND: Do major news organisations report this? TRACE: Does the 'leaked document' exist and is it verifiable? Classic misinformation tactics: extreme claim, conspiracy framing, emotional language, vague evidence.

quiz.q: The SIFT method stands for:
Lateral reading means:
options: Reading from multiple sources about the same topic
Checking a source by reading what others say about it externally
Reading two newspaper articles side by side

media_literacy.label: Media Literacy
media_literacy.description: Navigate news, social media, and advertising with a critical eye.

lessons.title: How to Spot Fake News
lessons.explanation:
Misinformation (false information, not necessarily intentional) and disinformation (deliberately false information) spread rapidly through social media. Key indicators of unreliable news:

• CLICKBAIT HEADLINES: Exaggerated, emotional, designed to provoke clicks rather than inform.
• PROPAGANDA: Information designed to promote a particular political agenda or group.
• MEDIA BIAS: All sources have some perspective — understanding a source's perspective helps assess its reporting.
• ADVERTISING VS NEWS: Can you tell the difference between paid content and editorial journalism?
lessons.example: A viral social media post claims: 'Scientists prove eating chocolate every day cures cancer!' Red flags: no named scientists, no link to a study, extreme claim, emotional headline.
lessons.exercise: Apply the SIFT method to this headline: 'Government secretly adds chemicals to drinking water to control minds, leaked document reveals!'
lessons.exercise_answer: Stop and question the extreme claim. Investigate: Is this source reliable? Find better coverage: do established news sources report this? Trace the 'leaked document' — does it exist?

quiz.q: The SIFT method stands for:
Which is the BEST indicator that a news story might be unreliable?
options: It has no named sources and makes extreme claims

lessons.title: Advertising Techniques & Critical Viewing
lessons.explanation:
Advertisers use psychological techniques to influence purchasing decisions:

• BANDWAGON: Everyone is using this — don't be left out.
• CELEBRITY ENDORSEMENT: Famous people promote the product.
• EMOTIONAL APPEAL: Uses feelings (fear, love, aspiration) to bypass rational thinking.
• SCARCITY: 'Limited time offer!' creates urgency.
• AUTHORITY: 'Dentists recommend…'
• REPETITION: Repeated exposure increases familiarity and likeability.
• SOCIAL PROOF: 'Millions of customers' signals reliability.

Algorithms on social media amplify content that generates strong emotional reactions — including misleading content.
lessons.example: An advert shows a happy, successful family using a car. The car isn't making them happy — the advertiser is associating happiness with the product through emotional appeal.
lessons.exercise: Identify the advertising technique: 'Nine out of ten dentists recommend BrightSmile toothpaste.'
lessons.exercise_answer: Authority appeal. Follow-up questions: Who paid for the study? How were dentists selected? What were they asked to recommend compared to?

quiz.q: Which advertising technique plays on the fear of missing out?

ethics.label: Ethics & Moral Reasoning
ethics.description: Explore moral philosophy, ethical dilemmas, and how to reason about right and wrong.

lessons.title: Three Ethical Frameworks
lessons.explanation:
Philosophers have developed frameworks for deciding what is right and wrong:

CONSEQUENTIALISM (Utilitarianism): An action is right if it produces the best overall outcomes — the greatest good for the greatest number. Associated with philosophers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

DEONTOLOGY (Duty Ethics): Some actions are right or wrong regardless of their consequences. We have duties to follow moral rules. Associated with Immanuel Kant: act only according to principles you could wish to be universal laws.

VIRTUE ETHICS: Focuses on the character of the moral agent rather than rules or consequences. What would a virtuous person do? Associated with Aristotle.
lessons.example:
The Trolley Problem: A runaway trolley will kill 5 people. You can pull a lever to divert it to a side track where it will kill 1 person. Should you?

Consequentialist: Yes — 5 lives saved > 1 life lost.
Deontologist: No — you would be actively causing someone's death, which violates a moral duty.
Virtue ethicist: What would a courageous, compassionate person do?
lessons.exercise: A doctor can save 5 patients who need organ transplants by killing one healthy patient and using their organs. Is this ethical? Apply each framework.
lessons.exercise_answer: Consequentialist: Could argue yes — 5 lives saved > 1 lost. But most consequentialists would reject this because the rule 'doctors may kill patients' would have terrible long-term consequences. Deontological: No — it violates the duty not to kill and treats the healthy patient as a means, not an end. Virtue ethics: No virtuous doctor would do this — it violates compassion, justice, and medical integrity.

quiz.q: Utilitarianism holds that an action is right if:
options: It produces the greatest good for the greatest number

quiz.q: Kant's deontology emphasises:
options: The character of the person acting
Universal moral duties that apply regardless of outcomes

debate.label: Debate & Argumentation
debate.description: Structure arguments, identify fallacies in live debate, and argue effectively.

lessons.title: Structuring a Strong Argument
lessons.explanation:
A well-structured argument follows the PEEL method:

• POINT: State your main claim clearly.
• EVIDENCE: Provide specific facts, statistics, examples, or expert opinion to support it.
• EXPLANATION: Explain how the evidence supports your point.
• LINK: Connect back to the overall argument or question.

For debate, also prepare to:
• ANTICIPATE COUNTERARGUMENTS: What would opponents say? How would you respond?
• REBUT: Directly address and counter the opposing argument.

COMMON FALLACIES IN DEBATE:
• Appeal to emotion (exploiting feelings rather than logic)
• Slippery slope ('if we allow X, soon Y and Z will happen')
• False cause (assuming A caused B because they happened together)
• Hasty generalisation (drawing a conclusion from too few examples)
lessons.example:
Point: Homework should be limited to 30 minutes per day for primary school students.
Evidence: Research by Harris Cooper found that excessive homework in primary school has no positive effect on academic achievement and increases stress.
Explanation: If homework doesn't improve outcomes and causes stress, it is counterproductive at this age.
Link: Therefore, limiting homework protects wellbeing without harming learning.
lessons.exercise: Identify the fallacy: 'If we allow students to use calculators in exams, soon nobody will learn any maths at all and our society will collapse.'
lessons.exercise_answer: Slippery slope fallacy — it assumes a chain of extreme consequences from a modest change without evidence for each step in the chain.

quiz.q: The PEEL structure stands for:
Which is an example of a slippery slope fallacy?
options: 'If we ban plastic straws, within 5 years all plastic will be banned and civilisation will end'

ai_literacy.label: AI Literacy
ai_literacy.description: Understand what AI is, how it works, its limitations, and how to use it responsibly.

lessons.title: What AI Is — and What It Isn't
lessons.explanation:
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) refers to computer systems that perform tasks that normally require human intelligence — such as recognising images, translating languages, or generating text.

MACHINE LEARNING: AI systems learn from large amounts of data rather than being explicitly programmed. They find patterns in data.

LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS (LLMs): AI systems trained on vast amounts of text. They predict what text comes next, making them good at writing-like tasks. They do not 'understand' in the way humans do.

What AI is NOT:
• Not conscious or sentient — it doesn't have feelings or experiences.
• Not infallible — it can confidently give wrong answers ('hallucinations').
• Not neutral — it reflects biases in its training data.
• Not magic — it is mathematics applied to patterns in data.
lessons.example: A chatbot that answers questions about history is predicting statistically likely responses based on text patterns — it is not 'thinking about' history. If the training data contained errors or biases, the chatbot will reproduce them.
lessons.exercise: Why is it important to verify information given by an AI chatbot?
lessons.exercise_answer: AI chatbots can 'hallucinate' — produce plausible-sounding but incorrect information. They predict statistically likely text, not necessarily true text. They should be used as a starting point, not a final source, and claims should be verified with reliable, primary sources.

quiz.q: AI 'hallucination' means:
options: AI generates incorrect but confident-sounding information
AI imagines things like humans do

quiz.q: Large Language Models work by:
options: Looking up answers in a database
Predicting statistically likely text based on patterns
Searching the internet in real time

lessons.title: Bias in AI & Responsible Use
lessons.explanation:
AI systems can perpetuate and amplify biases present in their training data.

EXAMPLES OF AI BIAS:
• Facial recognition systems have been shown to work less accurately on darker skin tones because training data underrepresented these groups.
• Hiring algorithms trained on past hiring data can discriminate against groups that were historically underrepresented.
• Language models may associate certain professions with particular genders based on historical patterns in text.

RESPONSIBLE AI USE:
• Be transparent: Disclose when AI has helped create your work if required.
• Verify: Always check AI outputs against reliable sources.
• Think critically: AI tools reflect the biases of their creators and training data.
• Privacy: Avoid sharing personal or sensitive data with AI tools.
• Intellectual property: AI-generated content raises questions about authorship and copyright.
lessons.example: An image-generating AI, if trained mostly on Western art, will produce images that reflect Western visual traditions when asked for 'a person' — showing how training data shapes outputs.
lessons.exercise: If an AI job-screening tool was trained on hiring decisions from the last 30 years, what biases might it perpetuate? What would you do to address this?
lessons.exercise_answer: Historical hiring data likely underrepresents women, ethnic minorities, and people with disabilities in senior roles. The AI would likely favour applicants similar to those historically hired. To address this: audit outputs for disparate impact; diversify training data; ensure human oversight of decisions; test for bias across demographic groups before deployment.

quiz.q: AI bias often comes from:
options: Intentional programming by engineers to be unfair

quiz.q: When using AI tools for schoolwork, responsible practice includes:
options: Using AI outputs without checking them
Verifying AI outputs against reliable sources and disclosing use when required
Sharing all personal data to get better results
